findings.description: The check is too broad. `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is true for any part containing any SafeSelector placeholder, and SafeSelector also creates placeholders for attribute selectors (`[attr=val]`) and for escapes that are not hex escapes (`\:`). It does not check that the part ends in a hex escape. If such a part is followed by a space and a descendant selector starting with a hex character (a-f or 0-9), the combinator is skipped. Examples are `[disabled] div`, `input[type=text] a`, and `.one\:two .abc`. These are no longer split and scoped as separate compound selectors, so the output scoping attributes are wrong (for example `[disabled] div[contenta]` instead of `[disabled][contenta] div[contenta]`). This regresses common selectors.

The check is too broad. It only tests that the part contains any `__ph-N__` placeholder and that the next character is a hex digit. SafeSelector turns every backslash escape into a placeholder, including non-hex escapes like `\:` and `\/`. So `.md\:flex div {}` or `.sm\:foo a {}` becomes `.md__ph-0__flex div`, the part matches the placeholder, and `d` or `a` passes the hex test. The descendant combinator is then skipped and the selectors are merged. The scoping attribute is not added to the first compound selector, and the combinator handling is wrong. This regresses previously working selectors, such as Tailwind-style classes followed by a descendant starting with a-f or a digit. The check should confirm that the placeholder is at the end of the part and that it stands for a hex escape. It also applies to non-space separators such as `>`, `+` and `~`, where `selector[res.index+1]` is not the separator's trailing character.

The `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally when the module loads. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework defines these globals, for example when the file is pulled into a bundle or loaded in a non-test context, it throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. The old code skipped registration safely in that case.

The `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. If `@angular/core/testing` is imported where no test framework globals exist (for example a server bundle or catalog, or a non-test tool that loads the module), this throws `ReferenceError: beforeEach is not defined`. Previously the module loaded without error in those environments. A `typeof beforeEach !== 'undefined'` guard is needed.

`collectDeferredSymbols` sets `deferBlockDep.isDeferrable` and `importPath`, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport`. It stays at the initial `false`. The per-defer-block dependency functions (`TemplateDefinitionBuilder` and `createDeferDepsFns`) read `dep.isDefaultImport`, so for a default-imported component they still emit `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m => m.default`. At runtime the lazily loaded dependency resolves to `undefined` and the deferred content breaks. Only the `deferrableTypes` map and `setClassMetadataAsync` get the correct `default` access.

`isDefaultImport` is computed per import declaration, not per identifier. `import Cmp, {Other} from './x'` has `namedBindings` set, so the default-imported `Cmp` is treated as a named import and gets `m.Cmp` instead of `m.default`. Conversely, the named `Other` could be misclassified if the check were changed. A mixed import therefore produces an incorrect dynamic-import accessor.

isDefaultImport() only checks that the import clause has no namedBindings. For a mixed import such as `import CmpA, {CmpB} from './x'`, namedBindings is defined, so a deferred default-imported symbol is reported as not default. The generated code is then `m => m.CmpA` instead of `m => m.default`, which resolves to undefined at runtime. The same failure happens for `import {default as CmpA}`. The check is per declaration and never identifies which binding is the deferred symbol.

copyEventListenerOptions uses `{...options}`, which copies only own enumerable properties. Options objects that supply `capture`, `once` or `passive` through the prototype chain or as accessors on a class instance (for example `Object.create({capture:true})`) will silently lose those values. Only `signal` is special-cased. The native listener is then registered with different options than the caller asked for. This is an edge-case regression.

The constructor condition is inverted: `if (!this.isAnchorElement) { this.subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary(); } else { this.setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0'); }`. For non-anchor elements, the subscribe call returns immediately because it bails when `!isAnchorElement`, and `setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0')` is never called. Non-anchor hosts such as `<div routerLink>` therefore lose their default `tabindex="0"` and become unreachable by keyboard. For anchors, `setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl` is a no-op, so the else branch does nothing useful.

The subscription condition is wrong. `!this.queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(defaultQueryParamsHandling)` subscribes when the link does NOT depend on router state. It skips the subscription when the router-wide `defaultQueryParamsHandling` is 'merge' or 'preserve' and the link sets no handling of its own. In that case the href depends on the current URL's query params but is never updated on NavigationEnd, so the href goes stale after navigation.

The constructor condition was inverted. The original code subscribed for anchor elements and called `setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0')` for non-anchor elements. Now `if (!this.isAnchorElement)` calls `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary()`, which returns immediately for non-anchors, so it does nothing. The `else` branch then sets `tabindex="0"` on anchor elements and never on non-anchor elements. Non-anchor `routerLink` hosts such as `<div routerLink>` lose their default tabindex and are no longer keyboard-focusable. Native anchors get an unwanted tabindex.

The subscription condition for the case with no `queryParamsHandling` is inverted. `!this.queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(defaultQueryParamsHandling)` subscribes to NavigationEnd when the default handling does NOT depend on router state. It skips subscribing when the router default is 'merge' or 'preserve', which is when the href does depend on the current query params. In that case the href goes stale after navigation. The `!` before `dependsOnRouterState` should be removed.

The helper is not a drop-in replacement for the previous `.toPromise()`. `toPromise()` resolved with the last emitted value, or `undefined` if the source completed empty. `first()` resolves with the first value and rejects with `EmptyError` if the source completes without emitting. An observable returned from a `redirectTo` function (or from `canLoad`/`loadChildren`) that emits several values or completes empty now behaves differently. Empty completion becomes a rejected promise, and the last value is no longer the one used. This is an edge case, and the first-value behavior is probably intended.

`leavingNodes` is keyed by `TNode`, which is shared by every instance of a component or template. The new rule "leaving element is in a different DOM parent → cancel" therefore cancels leave animations that belong to unrelated instances. If one instance's animated root is leaving in parent P1 while another instance of the same component is inserted into parent P2 (e.g. components in different containers, or different `@for` rows), the first element is force-ended with a cancel `animationend` and removed immediately. The leave animation is cut short and the element disappears early. The diff has no way to tell the overlay/portal case apart from this one.

`cancelLeavingNodes` now runs after every insert of a node with a tracked leaving element, and it cancels whenever the leaving element is the new element's `previousSibling`. With `@for`, removing the last item (which starts a leave animation) and adding a new item in the same or a later change detection inserts the new item right after the leaving one. The leaving element then counts as the "previous sibling" and is killed abruptly. Those are different logical items, not an `@if` toggle, so the leave animation is cut short.

The "different DOM parent" heuristic cancels and force-removes leaving elements that belong to unrelated instances. `leavingNodes` is keyed by `tNode`, and a `tNode` is shared by every instance of a component or template. If instance A is animating out in parent P1 and instance B of the same template is inserted into a different parent P2, B's insert treats A as an overlay duplicate. It dispatches a cancel `animationend` and removes A's element, cutting off A's leave animation early. This is a regression for any list of components that each have `animate.leave` and live in different containers.

`cancelLeavingNodes` runs on every Insert and cancels any leaving element that is the new node's `previousSibling`. This also fires for `@for` or ViewContainerRef cases where a different item is added right after one that is still animating out. For example, removing the last item B and then appending a new item C puts C before the anchor, directly after B. B's leave animation is then cancelled and B is removed, even though the comment says same-parent leaving items are left alone. The adjacency test cannot tell "same logical node re-created" from "unrelated new item".

On Detach, the element is added to `leavingNodes` whenever the tNode has leave animations, before `runLeaveAnimationsWithCallback` runs. If the leave animation does not run or finish normally, for example when animations are disabled or the element is removed some other way, the entry may never be cleared. That leaves stale element references that keep detached DOM alive. The `includes` check also makes each `trackLeavingNodes` call O(n).

The removal of pending enter animations from the queue when a node starts leaving has been dropped, along with `removeAnimationsFromQueue`. If a node is created and destroyed before the next animation-frame flush, its queued enter animation functions still run against an element that is already leaving or detached. This can apply enter classes or listeners to a node being removed and interfere with the leave animation.

The old code interpolated `position` (a number[]) into a quoted string, so the inspected page received the comma-separated form "0,1,2". The new `stringifyAndEscape(position)` passes the string "[0,1,2]" instead. `findConstructorByPosition` and `findDomElementByPosition` parse their argument with `split(',')` and `parseInt`, so the bracketed form yields NaN indices ("[0" and "2]"). This breaks view-source and select-DOM-element for components. The same format change applies to `selectDomElement`.

The position argument changes format. Before, `'${position}'` interpolated the number[] into a string like "0,1,2". Now `stringifyAndEscape(position)` passes the string "[0,1,2]". If `findConstructorByPosition` still parses the comma-separated form (split(',') and Number), the first and last elements become "[0" and "2]" and parse to NaN. View source would then fail to find the element. The receiving side is not updated in this diff.

`findDomElementByPosition` now receives "[0,1,2]" instead of the comma-joined "0,1,2". If it still splits on commas, the parsed indices are NaN. Selecting a DOM element from the component tree would then break. The receiving function is not updated in this diff.
